title: Plant Morphology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200L Plant Morphology curriculum: external form and modifications of root, stem, leaf, inflorescence, flower, fruit and seed in angiosperms.

questions.question: The radicle of a germinating seed develops into the:
questions.correct_answer: Primary root
questions.explanation: The radicle is the embryonic root; it elongates and develops into the primary (tap) root.

questions.question: A fibrous root system, typical of most monocotyledons, arises from:
options: Adventitious roots replacing the short-lived radicle
Continued growth of the primary root only
Lateral branching of a single dominant taproot
questions.correct_answer: Adventitious roots replacing the short-lived radicle
questions.explanation: In monocots the radicle is short-lived and is replaced by numerous adventitious roots of similar size forming a fibrous mat.

questions.question: Pneumatophores, seen in mangrove plants such as Rhizophora and Avicennia, are root modifications for:
questions.correct_answer: Gaseous exchange in waterlogged soil
questions.explanation: Pneumatophores are negatively geotropic roots that grow upward out of anaerobic mud to allow the plant to obtain atmospheric oxygen.

questions.question: Root nodules containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium) are characteristic of plants in which family?
questions.correct_answer: Fabaceae (Leguminosae)
questions.explanation: Legumes form a symbiotic relationship with Rhizobium bacteria housed in specialised root nodules that fix atmospheric nitrogen.

questions.question: Which root modification is exhibited by the tuberous roots of cassava (Manihot esculenta)?
questions.correct_answer: Storage of food reserves
questions.explanation: Cassava roots swell with stored starch, forming fleshy tuberous roots used as a food reserve for the plant.

questions.question: A stem is distinguished from a root morphologically by the presence of:
options: Nodes and internodes bearing leaves and buds
questions.correct_answer: Nodes and internodes bearing leaves and buds
questions.explanation: Stems are organised into nodes (where leaves/buds arise) and internodes, a feature roots lack.

questions.question: The underground stem of ginger (Zingiber officinale) is an example of a:
questions.correct_answer: Rhizome
questions.explanation: Ginger has a horizontally growing underground stem (rhizome) with nodes, scale leaves and buds, distinguishing it from roots.

questions.question: A corm, as found in Colocasia (cocoyam), differs from a bulb mainly because a corm is:
options: A solid, swollen stem base with thin scale leaves
Composed mainly of fleshy overlapping leaf bases
An underground root swollen with food
A stem that grows entirely horizontally along the soil surface
questions.correct_answer: A solid, swollen stem base with thin scale leaves
questions.explanation: A corm is a vertical, solid stem structure with food stored in the stem tissue itself, covered by dry scale leaves, unlike a bulb where fleshy leaf bases store the food.

questions.question: The stem tendrils used by Passiflora (passion flower) for climbing are modified:
questions.correct_answer: Axillary shoots
questions.explanation: In Passiflora, the tendril develops from an axillary bud as a modified stem branch that coils around supports.

questions.question: Cladodes (phylloclades), such as those found in some cacti, are:
options: Flattened, photosynthetic stems that replace leaf function
questions.correct_answer: Flattened, photosynthetic stems that replace leaf function
questions.explanation: Cladodes are green, flattened stems that take over photosynthesis when leaves are reduced to spines, common in xerophytes.

questions.question: A leaf is generally described as dorsiventral (bifacial) when:
options: Its upper and lower surfaces differ in structure and appearance
questions.correct_answer: Its upper and lower surfaces differ in structure and appearance
questions.explanation: Dorsiventral leaves have distinct adaxial (upper) and abaxial (lower) surfaces, typical of most dicot leaves.

questions.question: Reticulate (net-like) venation is typically associated with:
questions.correct_answer: Dicotyledonous leaves
questions.explanation: Dicot leaves typically show reticulate venation with a network of veins branching from a midrib, unlike the parallel venation of most monocots.

questions.question: A leaf with a single, undivided lamina, such as that of mango, is termed:
questions.correct_answer: Simple
questions.explanation: A simple leaf has one continuous blade that is not divided into separate leaflets, whether or not its margin is lobed.

questions.question: In a pinnately compound leaf, such as that of neem (Azadirachta indica), the leaflets are arranged:
options: Along both sides of a common central axis (rachis)
Radiating from a single point at the tip of the petiole
In two opposite rows without a rachis
questions.correct_answer: Along both sides of a common central axis (rachis)
questions.explanation: Pinnately compound leaves bear leaflets arranged on either side of an elongated rachis, resembling a feather.

questions.question: Palmately compound leaves, as in Carica papaya (pawpaw) and silk cotton (Ceiba), have leaflets that:
options: Radiate from a single point at the apex of the petiole
Are fused into one continuous blade
questions.correct_answer: Radiate from a single point at the apex of the petiole
questions.explanation: In palmate compound leaves all leaflets attach at one common point, like fingers spreading from a palm.

questions.question: The arrangement of leaves on a stem is known as:
questions.correct_answer: Phyllotaxy
questions.explanation: Phyllotaxy describes the pattern of leaf arrangement (alternate, opposite, whorled, spiral) along the stem.

questions.question: In opposite decussate phyllotaxy, successive pairs of leaves are:
options: At right angles to the pair above and below
Parallel to the pair above and below
Arranged spirally at a fixed angle
In whorls of three or more
questions.correct_answer: At right angles to the pair above and below
questions.explanation: Decussate arrangement places each opposite pair of leaves at 90 degrees to the pairs immediately above and below it, common in the Lamiaceae.

questions.question: Stipules, when present, are typically found:
options: At the base of the petiole, one on each side
At the tip of the leaf blade
questions.correct_answer: At the base of the petiole, one on each side
questions.explanation: Stipules are paired lateral outgrowths at the base of the petiole, seen for example in roses and legumes.

questions.question: Leaf tendrils, as seen in Pisum sativum (garden pea), are modifications where:
options: Part of the compound leaf is modified into a coiling structure for climbing
The whole leaf becomes a spine
The lamina becomes fleshy for storage
questions.correct_answer: Part of the compound leaf is modified into a coiling structure for climbing
questions.explanation: In the pea, the terminal leaflets of the pinnately compound leaf are modified into tendrils that help the plant climb.

questions.question: Leaf spines, as in cacti, primarily serve to:
options: Reduce water loss and deter herbivores
questions.correct_answer: Reduce water loss and deter herbivores
questions.explanation: Reducing the leaf to a spine minimises transpirational surface area in arid conditions while also providing defence against grazing.

questions.question: An inflorescence in which the main axis continues to grow and produces flowers laterally in acropetal succession is termed:
questions.correct_answer: Racemose
questions.explanation: In racemose inflorescences the main axis keeps growing indefinitely, with the oldest flowers at the base and youngest near the tip (acropetal order).

questions.question: A cymose inflorescence differs from a racemose one in that:
options: The main axis terminates in a flower, and growth continues via lateral branches
Flowers are borne directly on the main stem without pedicels
It always develops into a fleshy fruit
questions.correct_answer: The main axis terminates in a flower, and growth continues via lateral branches
questions.explanation: Cymose (definite) inflorescences have the apical meristem used up in forming a terminal flower, so subsequent flowers arise from lateral axes below it.

questions.question: The capitulum (head), typical of the Asteraceae (e.g., sunflower), consists of:
options: Many small sessile florets crowded on a flattened receptacle
A single large flower with numerous petals
Flowers arranged in a flat-topped raceme
A spike enclosed by a spathe
questions.correct_answer: Many small sessile florets crowded on a flattened receptacle
questions.explanation: A capitulum is a specialised racemose inflorescence where numerous tiny florets are packed on a broad receptacle, surrounded by bracts, giving the appearance of a single flower.

questions.question: A spadix, as seen in the aroid family (e.g., Anthurium, Colocasia), is characterised by:
options: A fleshy spike enclosed or subtended by a large bract called a spathe
Flowers borne on pedicels of equal length arising from one point
A flat-topped cluster of stalked flowers
Whorled flowers with no central axis
questions.correct_answer: A fleshy spike enclosed or subtended by a large bract called a spathe
questions.explanation: The spadix is a thickened, fleshy spike of small flowers typically enclosed by a conspicuous spathe, a hallmark of the Araceae.

questions.question: The four whorls of a typical complete flower, from outermost to innermost, are arranged as:
questions.correct_answer: Calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium
questions.explanation: A complete flower has, from outside in, the sepals (calyx), petals (corolla), stamens (androecium), and carpels (gynoecium).

questions.question: A flower that can be bisected into two equal mirror-image halves along only one plane is described as:
questions.correct_answer: Zygomorphic (irregular)
questions.explanation: Zygomorphic flowers, such as those of the Fabaceae, have bilateral symmetry with only one plane of symmetry, unlike actinomorphic (radially symmetrical) flowers.

questions.question: The arrangement of sepals or petals in a floral bud before it opens is called:
questions.correct_answer: Aestivation
questions.explanation: Aestivation refers to the way floral organs overlap or are arranged relative to one another within the bud.

questions.question: A hypogynous flower is one in which the ovary is:
options: Superior, with other floral parts inserted below it
Inferior, with other floral parts inserted above it
questions.correct_answer: Superior, with other floral parts inserted below it
questions.explanation: In hypogynous flowers the receptacle is convex and the ovary sits above the point of attachment of sepals, petals and stamens, giving a superior ovary.

questions.question: In an epigynous flower, such as that of guava or a member of the Cucurbitaceae, the ovary is described as:
questions.correct_answer: Inferior
questions.explanation: In epigynous flowers the receptacle grows up and around the ovary, fusing with it, so other floral whorls appear to arise above the ovary, which is termed inferior.

questions.question: Axile placentation, seen in Hibiscus, is characterised by ovules attached to:
options: A central axis formed by the fused margins of a multilocular ovary
The inner wall of a single-chambered ovary
A free central column not connected to the ovary wall
The placenta running along the ovary wall in a single line
questions.correct_answer: A central axis formed by the fused margins of a multilocular ovary
questions.explanation: Axile placentation occurs when carpels fuse to form a multi-chambered ovary with ovules borne on a central axis where the septa meet.

questions.question: Parietal placentation, seen in Cucurbitaceae and Brassicaceae, describes ovules attached to:
options: The inner ovary wall in a unilocular ovary
The apex of the ovary only
The base of the ovary only
questions.correct_answer: The inner ovary wall in a unilocular ovary
questions.explanation: In parietal placentation, ovules are borne on the ovary wall (on the fused carpel margins) within a single chamber.

questions.question: A drupe, exemplified by the mango fruit, is a fleshy fruit characterised by:
options: A fleshy mesocarp and a hard, stony endocarp enclosing the seed
Numerous small seeds embedded in a fleshy receptacle
A papery pericarp that splits along one suture
questions.correct_answer: A fleshy mesocarp and a hard, stony endocarp enclosing the seed
questions.explanation: Drupes have a three-layered pericarp: thin exocarp, fleshy mesocarp, and a hard lignified endocarp forming the 'stone' around the seed.

questions.question: A legume (pod), such as that of Fabaceae, is a dry dehiscent fruit that splits along:
options: Both the dorsal and ventral sutures
questions.correct_answer: Both the dorsal and ventral sutures
questions.explanation: A legume develops from a single carpel and dehisces along both sutures (dorsal and ventral) to release the seeds, distinguishing it from a follicle which splits along only one suture.

questions.question: The pepo, a fruit type found in the Cucurbitaceae (e.g., melon, cucumber), is best described as:
options: A fleshy berry-like fruit with a hard rind formed from an inferior ovary
A dry, one-seeded fruit with a hard pericarp
A dehiscent fruit splitting into several segments
questions.correct_answer: A fleshy berry-like fruit with a hard rind formed from an inferior ovary
questions.explanation: A pepo is a specialised berry with a thickened, hardened outer rind (from the receptacle and exocarp) developing from an inferior ovary, typical of cucurbits.

questions.question: An achene, such as that of sunflower, is a dry indehiscent fruit in which:
options: The single seed is attached to the pericarp at only one point and is easily separated from it
The pericarp is fused completely to the seed coat
Numerous seeds are enclosed within a fleshy pericarp
The fruit splits open at maturity to release seeds
questions.correct_answer: The single seed is attached to the pericarp at only one point and is easily separated from it
questions.explanation: In an achene the thin pericarp encloses a single seed but remains free from the seed coat except at one point of attachment, unlike a caryopsis where they are fused.

questions.question: A caryopsis, the characteristic fruit of grasses (Poaceae) such as maize, differs from an achene in that:
options: The pericarp is completely fused to the seed coat
It is a fleshy, multi-seeded fruit
It dehisces along a single suture
It develops from multiple fused carpels with separate locules
questions.correct_answer: The pericarp is completely fused to the seed coat
questions.explanation: In a caryopsis (grain), the thin pericarp is fused inseparably to the seed coat, unlike the achene where the two remain distinct.

questions.question: A false fruit (pseudocarp), such as the apple or cashew, is one in which:
options: The main edible/fleshy part develops from tissue other than the ovary, such as the receptacle
Only the ovary wall contributes to the fruit
The fruit is formed without fertilisation
questions.correct_answer: The main edible/fleshy part develops from tissue other than the ovary, such as the receptacle
questions.explanation: In pseudocarps, accessory tissue (commonly the receptacle) forms the bulk of the fruit, while the true ovary contributes only a smaller part (e.g., the core in apple).

questions.question: In a dicotyledonous seed such as the bean, the two cotyledons chiefly function to:
options: Store food reserves for the developing embryo
Anchor the seed to the soil
questions.correct_answer: Store food reserves for the developing embryo
questions.explanation: In non-endospermic dicot seeds like the bean, food reserves are stored in the fleshy cotyledons, which nourish the embryo during germination.

questions.question: The micropyle of a seed is significant because it:
options: Marks the point of pollen tube entry and later allows water uptake during germination
Is the scar left by detachment from the funicle
Stores the bulk of the endosperm
questions.correct_answer: Marks the point of pollen tube entry and later allows water uptake during germination
questions.explanation: The micropyle is a small pore in the integuments through which the pollen tube entered during fertilisation; it later serves as the main site of water entry during imbibition.

questions.question: Epigeal germination, as seen in the bean (Phaseolus), is characterised by:
options: Elongation of the hypocotyl, lifting the cotyledons above the soil
Elongation of the epicotyl, leaving the cotyledons below the soil
Cotyledons remaining permanently underground and swelling
questions.correct_answer: Elongation of the hypocotyl, lifting the cotyledons above the soil
questions.explanation: In epigeal germination the hypocotyl elongates and arches, pulling the cotyledons up above the soil surface, where they may become photosynthetic.

questions.question: Hypogeal germination, as seen in maize and pea, is characterised by:
options: The cotyledon(s) remaining below the soil surface while the epicotyl elongates
The cotyledons being raised above the soil on an elongated hypocotyl
The radicle growing upward instead of downward
questions.correct_answer: The cotyledon(s) remaining below the soil surface while the epicotyl elongates
questions.explanation: In hypogeal germination the hypocotyl stays short, so the cotyledon(s) remain underground, and it is the epicotyl that elongates to push the plumule above the soil.

questions.question: Runners (stolons), as seen in Ipomoea (sweet potato vine) and strawberry, are a means of:
options: Vegetative propagation via horizontally creeping stems that root at the nodes
questions.correct_answer: Vegetative propagation via horizontally creeping stems that root at the nodes
questions.explanation: Runners are slender stems growing along the soil surface that develop roots and new shoots at the nodes, producing genetically identical daughter plants.

questions.question: Suckers, used in the vegetative propagation of banana (Musa spp.), arise from:
options: Adventitious buds on the underground rhizome/corm
Seeds shed at the base of the plant
The apical bud of the main stem
Modified leaves at the base of the plant
questions.correct_answer: Adventitious buds on the underground rhizome/corm
questions.explanation: Banana suckers develop from lateral buds on the underground corm-like rhizome and can be separated to establish new plants identical to the parent.
